This is the story on how this game saved me over $2,100 in repairs IRL. 

I’ve been a firearm owner ever since I was a kid. My father bought me my first .22 rifle when I was twelve. After I became an adult and joined the US ARMY (11B) I got more serious about my collection. It was not until I started my own company and could start buying seriously expensive firearms that I really took off. 
I ran into a dilemma a few months back. I had my Fully Automatic Browning M2 .50 and I could not get the charging handle to move all the way to the rear. I tried my best to ask around but nothing worked. I was about to throw in the towel and take it to my local gun smith when I remembered that World of guns existed. After going through the in-game play, I found out that it was a simple two-inch piece of metal that I had not put back in the proper place. After talking to the local gun smith. He told me that the repairs would have cost me almost $2,100 because of how much time it would have taken him along with the peace being ordered. 
World of Guns is so detailed and in-depth. The developers really went to full lengths to make it as realistic as possible. They must have the actual firearms in the studio to get the attention to detail that they have. I salute the developers for going the extra mile and giving us firearms fans something to be really excited about.

The game is NOT that interesting to spend that much time on it, and it's clearly not worth the 49.99 "Guns Full Access" price which doesn't even get you all that much if you read the fine print (there are 12 other DLCs for this other than that).

Don't waste your time/money on this piece of garbage.

It's just great because we've got so many games that have guns in it, yet many people haven't touched a real gun.(except in the US)
When we want to know how it works, we just don't have a clue.
Yes, we've got youtube and many other sites, but none of them are interactive.
When you want to know that specific part where they don't explain to you, you've got no idea.

So there is this game.

There's disassembly, motion check, X-ray mode, anything you'll need to learn how it works.

Not going to lie- this is a pretty awesome game. At first I was skeptical due to the fact that you have to pay 50 dollars to buy all the guns unlocked, plus 10 dollars for the gun range. Because of this I thought the "free" really meant "demo," which after playing the tutorial I found out it wasn't a "pay to get more play" game. Instead, you gain experience from doing certain things to the original gun you get such as disassembling, assembling, and time trials. These activities merit you experience with which you can aquire more guns. The second gun you get, the Colt, is about 2,000 experience, so after you do a few tasks for the tutorial you will have just enough experience to buy the Colt. The unlocking in this game is sort of like a tech tree where as you can't unlock more guns until you unlock the previous gun, and as you get higher in the tree it branches off. For instance you unlock the Colt, then the MP5, then that branches off to the Bretta or Tech 9. After you complete certain tasks you gain the power to shoot the gun, customize the gun, and watch it in x-ray and slow motion to see all the working parts. To sum everything all up, if you love guns and love learning more about them, this is the game for you!

This is a fun little game for the first few hours, and then a frustrating, rage-inducing, paywall-blocking simulator.

If you don't like minigames where one mistake sends you back to the beginning, this game isn't for you.

If you don't like spending ludicrious amounts of money on in-game purchases, this game isn't for you.

If you don't like grinding for hours with little progress, this game isn't for you.

But if you have money and time to burn, and have an interest in guns, this MAY be for you. But then again, where's the fun in buying the full pack and unlocking everything immediately?

The game's objective is easily outlined and aptly described by its title:

You have a gun. You take the gun apart. You put the gun back together.

It begins with a field strip. Then a disassembly. Then a reassembly. The game holds your hand at that stage, so you get a rough idea of where you're going.

Then, after getting a run through how to work the gun, you get the Game modes, playing against the clock and your own ham-fistedness, trying to achieve a high score.

New guns are unlocked via experience points, which are effectively available infinitely, and with credits. A single credit is earned when you first reach the top spot in the leadboards for a gun. This means that there is a finite amount of credits to be had, and their spending should be well-considered.

Of course, there's another way to get credits and EXP, and that's where the microtransactions come in. I've not personally done this, but you can buy credits and EXP for real money. It is not, however, necessary.

As for the gameplay itself, it is for the most part fairly solid, though often overly particular about which bits can be taken off the gun at which point in time. Figuring this out is solely a matter of repetition, yet often a source of frustration. It's an incredibly grindy game, no two ways about it.

And I, personally, adore it. After a while I decided I'd be a good little blighter and give the devs some money as a show of support, so I bought the car pack.

The basic premise of this game is simple... dissassemble and reassemble every kind of gun imaginable. From notable historic models, to modern military pieces, even a few vehicles, and some skeletons, this game has a lot to offer anyone who loves fiddling with intricate models, and looking at how things work.

It's got a few negative quirks, though. As others have noted, the game is very unforgiving to those who don't want to pay for microtransactions. If you're just a casual player wanting to look at all the different models, expect to pay a lot.

Even if you're really into the puzzle aspects, expect to throw down a few dollars on occasion for that really nice model you want to try out.

Another negative is the inconsistency between models. Some models will require you to pull apart every single little screw, bolt, flange, and spring. Others will do most of the detail work for you, dissassembling large amounts of items with one click. It can be especially frustrating when trying to get the higher difficulty achievements, to figure out just how much attention to detail a specific model wants you to have. Planning and memorization are key.

If you like puzzles, though, and aren't afraid to shell out a few dollars now and then, pick this up. You'll be engrossed pretty quickly, I guarantee.
